articles.title: Meta, TikTok, Google sue California over child online safety restrictions
articles.summary: Meta, TikTok and Google filed separate lawsuits against California over a new law seeking to tighten restrictions on child social media usage, arguing the legislation violates the companies’ First Amendment rights. California’s bipartisan “Digital Age Assurance Act,” which goes into effect Jan. 1, bans social media platforms in the Sunshine State from providing “an addictive…
articles.body:
Meta, TikTok and Google filed separate lawsuits against California over a new law seeking to tighten restrictions on child social media usage, arguing the legislation violates the companies’ First Amendment rights.

California’s bipartisan “ Digital Age Assurance Act ,” which goes into effect Jan. 1, bans social media platforms in the Sunshine State from providing “an addictive feed” to users under the age of 16. It also requires these companies “implement reasonable measures” to prevent minors from accessing such features.

The three companies argued the bill violates both the First Amendment and the federal Communications Decency Act, which protects online platforms from being sued over third party content. However, the law, established in 1996, went into effect as social media was in its early infancy.

A spokesperson for California Attorney General Rob Bonta (D) said the office was reviewing the filings.

“Our office is committed to defending California’s commonsense laws to protect kids online,” the spokesperson said.

In Meta’s lawsuit , attorneys described the California law as an attempt to “appoint the State as the editor, curator and controller of online speech” and “override Meta’s editorial judgment about how to curate and display these billions of posts of third-party speech.”

According to The Associated Press , in TikTok’s filing, the company called the bill a “blatantly unconstitutional restriction on free expression that erodes the long-standing and protected practice of curating content based on user preferences, which bookstores, TV networks and streaming services all use.”

TikTok’s lawsuit went on to highlight the multiple safety measures it already has in place to protect young users.

Google, in its lawsuit , called on the state to defer restrictions on child social media usage to parents, referencing its own range of parental controls.

The legal challenge comes after tech company Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, along with Snapchat’s parent company Snap Inc. both settled lawsuits with teenagers alleging their platforms had adverse mental health effects. The two social media industry giants are also embroiled in a similar lawsuit in Los Angeles, in which plaintiffs allege their platforms are purposefully designed to be addictive.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg is expected to take the stand in this trial sometime in November.

The Los Angeles lawsuit targeted social media companies over the design of the platforms as opposed to the content.

Several tech industry leaders have agreed to multimillion dollar payouts to settle similar child online safety lawsuits.

In late August, Meta agreed to pay Texas more than $1 billion and pledged to add new restrictions to its platforms, such as blocking notifications during school hours and applying default daily time limits of two hours for users under the age of 18, which can only be lifted by a parent.

articles.title: Rubio places additional sanctions on Cuba, targeting ‘illicit’ shipping network
articles.summary: The Trump administration announced another wave of sanctions against Cuba Thursday, targeting 10 individuals and entities tied to the country’s government, military and oil industry. The State Department accused Cuba’s “ruling elite” in its announcement of “hoarding the island’s energy, shipping, and technology resources for its own enrichment, leaving the Cuban people to contend with…
articles.body:
The Trump administration announced another wave of sanctions against Cuba Thursday, targeting 10 individuals and entities tied to the country’s government, military and oil industry.

The State Department accused Cuba’s “ruling elite” in its announcement of “hoarding the island’s energy, shipping, and technology resources for its own enrichment, leaving the Cuban people to contend with blackouts, shortages, and a stagnant economy.”

The department said the sanctions target Cuban officials, state-owned businesses, Chinese suppliers providing equipment to its military and an offshore network involved in shipping crude oil amid the U.S.’s ongoing fuel embargo against the Caribbean nation. It also designated five vessels as blocked property.

“The Marxist regime in Havana relies on a web of state-owned enterprises, joint ventures, and offshore intermediaries to keep this system running,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in the release.

“Its foreign backers supply the military equipment that helps sustain the regime’s military forces and enable its brutal repression, while propping up its persistent efforts to threaten, infiltrate and subvert the American homeland,” he continued.

Among those sanctioned is Guillermo Faustino Rodriguez Lopez Calleja, whom the department identified as working with a network of offshore shipping companies transporting Cuban crude oil to and from the island.

The administration also sanctioned Any Rodriguez Lastres, whose mother — Ania Guillerma Lastres Morera — is the president of Cuba’s military-linked business conglomerate, Grupo de Administración Empresarial (GAESA), and was previously sanctioned by the U.S.

The Treasury Department also issued a rule allowing the U.S. to impose sanctions on foreign individuals and companies operating in Cuba’s electronics, manufacturing, marine and technology sectors.

“The Trump Administration will not stand by while the Cuban regime funnels the island’s resources to its military elite, while regime insiders and their family members profit from opaque offshore networks, and while Cuba continues to serve as a staging ground for a global coalition of hostile anti-American actors to threaten, spy on, and plot against the United States and its interests,” Rubio said.

The move broadens the range of foreign businesses that could face U.S. sanctions over their dealings with Cuba. It also adds to the administration’s efforts to choke off revenue to Cuba’s government and military-linked businesses while continuing to pressure Havana’s communist regime.

It also comes after Rubio offered Cubans the opportunity to enter into a discrete “partnership” with the CIA in late October and President Trump signaled plans to take military action against the island.

articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is reportedly not in consideration to replace Tennessee Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn’s (R) open Senate seat.

An Associated Press report , citing a person familiar with the matter who discussed the private conversations on condition of anonymity, stated that Hegseth is not being considered for the seat. Instead, Blackburn was focused on her transition to the governor’s mansion.

The person dismissed speculation about Hegseth taking Blackburn’s Senate seat as “baseless chatter.”

This comes after two sources told The Hill on Thursday that President Trump has been asking advisers and allies whether Hegseth’s standing following the midterms.

One of those sources said Hegseth is in “a lot of trouble,” while the other said it wasn’t clear how much his position was in jeopardy. Both spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive matters.

Though in public, Trump defended Hegseth , telling reporters on Wednesday he was not considering replacing the defense secretary, saying he was “doing a very good job,” but would be “very popular” if he filled Blackburn’s seat.

Hegseth, a former Army National Guard major, is interested in the open Tennessee Senate seat and has been campaigning behind the scenes for the post, The Hill previously reported.

A senior Pentagon official also stated that if Hegseth left his posting at the Pentagon, the process of replacing him would not be “practical,” pointing to the potential difficulty of finding a replacement who could be confirmed by the Senate during the lame-duck — and before Democrats take control of the upper chamber.

Outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) announced he would be introducing the eight articles of impeachment for Hegseth before the Kentucky senator left office.

The lawmaker has expressed that the only thing Hegseth could do to stop the effort would be to resign on his own accord .

Multiple other Tennessee politicians are interested in the seat including Reps. Tim Burchett (R-Tenn.) and Chuck Fleischmann (R-Tenn.), former Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs and former CoreCivic CEO Damon Hininger.

Burchett, particularly, has campaigned for Blackburn this election cycle.

articles.title: Palo Alto Networks in talks to buy AI agent security startup Clutch for $500M | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Clutch, backed by Lightspeed and SignalFire, was last valued at $85 million, according to a source.
articles.body:
Palo Alto Networks is in talks to acquire Clutch Security , a startup that secures AI agents’ access to company systems, for $500 million in cash plus additional milestone-based payouts, according to a person familiar with the discussions.

Three-year-old Clutch was last valued at $85 million when it raised a $20 million Series A round in January 2025, led by Lightspeed and SignalFire, according to our source. The startup is currently approaching $10 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR). That means the acquisition, if completed, would value Clutch at about 50 times its ARR, a standard way of pricing software companies.

Palo Alto Networks and Clutch Security did not respond to a request for comment. The Information was the first to report the acquisition discussions.

The high valuation is not an anomaly in a market increasingly focused on securing software against bad actors using AI to breach systems more easily. Upwind, a startup using AI to secure cloud infrastructure, recently turned down an acquisition offer from DataDog that valued it at roughly 40 times ARR, TechCrunch reported last week.

If the deal happens, it would be Palo Alto Networks’ seventh acquisition this year, according to PitchBook. The cybersecurity giant has a history of buying innovation rather than building it in-house, and it has ramped up dealmaking this year in response to rising AI-driven cyberattacks.

In September, Palo Alto Networks acquired Console, a two-year-old startup that uses AI agents to automate routine IT help desk tasks. The transaction valued Console at $500 million in stock and cash, TechCrunch reported. Other VC-backed companies that Palo Alto Networks has scooped up this year include NEA-backed Embrace, for $325 million ; Chronosphere, an observability platform backed by Greylock and Lux Capital, for $2.95 billion ; and Koi, a cyber startup backed by Battery and Team8, for $231 million , according to regulatory filings.

Several of Clutch’s competitors have also been acquired. Cyera, a cybersecurity startup valued at $12 billion earlier this year, acquired Oasis Security, which, like Clutch, focuses on managing AI agents’ access to systems, for $1 billion . Meanwhile, Cisco bought Menlo Ventures-backed Astrix for roughly $400 million , Calcalist reported.

articles.title: US Treasuries Stumble as Strong Labor Market Lifts Fed-Hike Bets
articles.summary: Treasuries dipped after an unexpected surge in US job growth led traders to add to wagers that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates when officials n...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Treasuries dipped after an unexpected surge in US job growth led traders to add to wagers that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates when officials next meet in December.

The declines on Friday pushed yields higher across maturities, with those on two-year notes — more sensitive to the outlook for the Fed's rate path than longer peers — up by as much as seven basis points to 4.54%. The 10-year yield was four basis points higher at 4.87% after data showed the US added 165,000 jobs in October, topping forecasts.

Traders maintained expectations of further rate hikes from the US central bank, pricing in a 70% chance of a quarter-point rate hike next month. All told, the market expects at least 40 basis points of additional tightening by September 2027.

Non-farm payrolls rose 165,000 last month, beating a forecast gain of 65,000, and the unemployment rate dipped to 4.1%. Revisions for prior months were positive and wage growth also picked up to 3.1% for the past year.

articles.title: Blockbuster October jobs report keeps Fed rate hike in play for December
articles.summary: Fed officials are already focused on higher inflation.
articles.body:
A much stronger-than-expected October jobs report solidifies expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates in December, as officials are already focused on higher inflation.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics report released Friday showed that 165,000 jobs were created in October , compared with expectations for around 70,000, as the unemployment rate edged down to 4.1%, compared with expectations for 4.2%. That's much higher than the average monthly gain of 48,000 over the past 12 months and well above the roughly 30,000 jobs needed to hold employment steady. Labor force participation inched up to a hair above expectations at 61.9%.

Job gains in both August and September were also revised higher by 84,000. The bulk of jobs added were in the sectors of professional and business services, healthcare, and transportation and warehousing. Manufacturing added 19,000 jobs.

While job gains are picking up, wage growth remains somewhat muted in comparison. Wages grew at 3.1% in October, compared with expectations for 2.9%.

Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh noted these dynamics following the last policy meeting, in which the Fed held rates steady . He pointed to payroll growth that is noticeably above last year's pace, the four-week moving average of unemployment insurance claims that continues to run at the lowest level in generations, and that "on the employment side of the Fed's dual mandate, conditions are quite positive."

"Yet Americans, of course, are still dealing with inflation that has been running above the Committee's objective for close to 6 years," he said. "It's our responsibility to get inflation down. That's the reason the FOMC's discussion over the last couple of days focused mainly on the price stability side of our remit."

Fed officials have noted that the job market is stable in recent comments and have said job growth is not adding to inflation.

Friday's jobs report raises the question of whether that could change if labor market growth continues at a higher pace. One report doesn't make a trend, and officials are not data-point dependent; they're focused on longer-term trends.

articles.title: TikTok’s For You page needs to change, says the EU
articles.summary: The EU Commission has accused TikTok of violating its rules surrounding online platforms with an algorithm that has a “rabbit hole effect” on users.
articles.body: The European Commission claims TikTok broke its online platform rules by offering a recommendation algorithm that creates a “rabbit hole effect” on users. In an announcement on Friday, the regulators allege TikTok’s algorithm can harm users with “endless and repeated exposure” to content related to sadness, isolation, or body image. The findings come months after the EU Commission declared that TikTok’s design is too “addictive.” While TikTok has implemented controls to mitigate the algorithm’s “rabbit hole effect,” the Commission says its preliminary findings suggest that they’re not effective. TikTok must now change the design of its For You feed, or else face fines of up to 6 percent of its global annual turnover. The platform is also facing pressure in the US, with lawmakers and a wave of lawsuits raising concerns about child safety. Since enacting the Digital Services Act in 2023 — a set of rules that hold tech companies legally accountable for their impact on users— the EU Commission has targeted several companies for allegedly violating the regulations, including X, Meta, Temu, and AliExpress. As reported by Politico, this is the first time the Commission has cited a recommendation algorithm as the reason for a breach. “Every time a user scrolls or likes a video on TikTok, the algorithm serves more of the same leading users down rabbit holes they cannot easily escape from,” Henna Virkkunen, the EU Commission’s executive vice president of tech sovereignty, security, and democracy, says in the press release. “Today’s preliminary findings show again that TikTok needs to step up its efforts to protect users’ well-being, including those of minors.”

articles.title: Tesla winding down Cybertruck production
articles.summary: Elon Musk announced on Friday that Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck next year after years of poor sales for the electric truck. In a post on the social platform X, the Tesla CEO said Cybertruck production will wind down at Gigafactory Texas in mid-2027 “to make room for increased Cybercab production.” The…
articles.body:
Elon Musk announced on Friday that Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck next year after years of poor sales for the electric truck.

In a post on the social platform X , the Tesla CEO said Cybertruck production will wind down at Gigafactory Texas in mid-2027 “to make room for increased Cybercab production.” The Texas factory is the only spot where Cybertruck is produced.

Tesla suffered months of low sales at the start of 2025, in part driven by backlash against Musk’s role within the Trump administration.

Kelley Blue Book estimated Cybertruck sales declined 48 percent from 2024 to 2025, and from January through September this year, sales were down 28 percent, The Associated Press reported.

Musk, a close ally of Trump and GOP mega-donor, led President Trump’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency, which conducted widespread layoffs and funding cuts across the federal government. The tech billionaire departed the government in May 2025, and after a brief falling out with the president, remains in Trump’s orbit.

Tesla’s showrooms also faced both peaceful and violent demonstrations last year, including vandalism, arson attacks and shootings.

Separately, Cybertruck also faced several recalls over safety concerns. In March 2025, U.S. safety regulators recalled almost every Cybertruck on the road due to an issue with its exterior panel.

articles.title: Just about anyone can rent access to White House IP addresses
articles.summary: A security firm has discovered residential proxy activity at the White House, potentially allowing outsiders to route their internet activity through the network.
articles.body: Someone at the White House appears to be running software that could enable outsiders to rent access on the presidential network for just “a few dollars,” as reported by Krebs on Security and The Register. That’s according to findings from the security firms Layer3 Intel and Synthient, which discovered residential proxy activity on the White House network. A residential proxy opens up a way for people to rent access to a home IP address and route their internet traffic through it, allowing them to conceal where their activity is actually coming from. Some apps and browser extensions include third-party software development kits (SDKs) that put proxy nodes on a user’s device — whether users know it or not. Third-party services can then sell access to the residential proxies on users’ devices. As noted by the cybersecurity firm Spur, people can legitimately use residential proxies for purposes like ad verification and quality assurance testing, but bad actors can also use them to bypass geolocation controls and defensive filters. Hackers have used residential proxies for all kinds of malicious activity, including to create botnets and carry out account takeovers. At the White House, Layer3 Intel found that 28 residential proxy services routed traffic out of the network from October 5th to November 3rd. It notes that this activity typically happens between 5PM ET and midnight. “That pattern suggests a person rather than a public guest Wi-Fi network: someone regularly on the White House network late into the evening, whose device is infected with a proxy SDK,” Layer3 says. The SDK in question might be linked to the watch party app Rave, according to Synthient, which says the app “bundles 12 proxy SDKs into the platform.” Synthient found “a number of Windows 10 and Windows 11 devices on the White House’s network beaconing to known proxy providers like Geonode, Infatica and Mellowtel.” As noted by Krebs on Security, Infatica is a proxy service founded by Vladimir Fomenko, the owner of King Servers, which was linked to 2016 cyberattacks on election systems in Illinois and Arizona. Layer3 warns that the residential proxy is “public access,” adding that “anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it.”

articles.title: DC official urges incoming Democratic governors to withdraw National Guard
articles.summary: Washington, D.C., officials are calling on incoming Democratic governors in five states that flipped blue to recall their National Guard troops from the nation’s capital, a move that could see some 628 guard members pulled from city streets come January. During a D.C. Council hearing on Thursday, council member Brooke Pinto (D) — the chair…
articles.body:
Washington, D.C., officials are calling on incoming Democratic governors in five states that flipped blue to recall their National Guard troops from the nation’s capital, a move that could see some 628 guard members pulled from city streets come January.

During a D.C. Council hearing on Thursday, council member Brooke Pinto (D) — the chair of the public safety committee — said she would soon send a letter on behalf of the council to ask the governors-elect in Iowa , Georgia, Nevada, Ohio and Texas to “immediately” withdraw their soldiers back to their states.

“It’s something they can do their first day in office,” she said.

“While we have asked all of the governors across the country in the past to pull back their troops, we’ve been met with a lot of resistance and a lot of governors who are following the lead from President Trump,” Pinto noted. “But we now have the opportunity, with Tuesday’s election results, to turn the tide of what we’re seeing in Washington, D.C., and to have some real accountability to the federal government.”

Some 3,100 National Guard troops are deployed in Washington as part of President Trump’s “Making the District of Columbia Safe and Beautiful” mission, which was announced last summer.

Of that number, just fewer than 760 troops are part of the D.C. National Guard — which is controlled by the sitting president — and 2,341 have been sent to the city by states and territories, nearly all of which are currently controlled by Republican governors, according to the mission’s joint task force .

While Texas, Ohio and Nevada currently only have one or two guard troops sent from each of their states, Georgia and Iowa can make a far bigger dent if they pull their 514 and 110 troops, respectively.

Should Alaska also flip to a Democratic governor — the race has yet to be called but has former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins (D) currently leading — it would mean an additional 34 guard members could be recalled.

Guard troops have been a common sight patrolling the streets of D.C. as part of their deployment, which began in August 2025, when the federal government ⁠temporarily took ​over the city’s law ​enforcement through ‌presidential executive order. The number of guard members has fluctuated over the course of a year, swelling to roughly 5,000 ahead of the Fourth of July.

That presence has worried local officials and residents, with Pinto saying Thursday that congressional leaders have been “unsympathetic to what we’ve been dealing with and, in some cases, directly hostile.”

“But after Tuesday night, the tide is turning,” she said.

Pinto also condemned a directive from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth late last month, which authorized the National Guard to begin using boats , up to 60 marked police cars and military tactical vehicles in D.C.

The action, which is sure to escalate the troops’ presence in the city and make it harder to discern between military members and law enforcement, is going in the “opposite direction” from what the city needs, she said.

Pinto also pressed the incoming congressional Democratic majority to more rigorously conduct oversight of federal policing activity in Washington, suggesting federal agents wear identifying badges and body cameras and that face coverings should be banned.

articles.title: Fed’s Daly Says More Rate Increases Likely Needed to Tame Prices
articles.summary: Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco President Mary Daly said more interest rate increases are likely to be needed to tame inflation, but she said it was to...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco President Mary Daly said more interest rate increases are likely to be needed to tame inflation, but she said it was too soon to know how much higher rates will need to go.

"My expectation is we're going to have to tighten policy further," Daly said Friday in an interview on CNBC. "Exactly when and how much is still to be decided because we just have to take all the variables that are coming in."

Daly said she supported the decision last week to hold the Fed's benchmark rate steady amid uncertainty about the economy, and that she also backed the decision to raise interest rates in September for the first time since 2023. While two policymakers dissented from the decision to hold rates last month because they preferred to raise them instead, several officials have expressed support for moving them up gradually.

articles.title: Lame-duck Congress might actually do something: speed up energy projects
articles.summary: A bipartisan group of legislators wants to make major changes to how federal agencies review major infrastructure projects, a move that could speed permitting for energy and data center projects while limiting public participation.
articles.body: A massive permitting bill that could help energy projects come online much quicker and potentially lower utility bills for Americans is advancing with bipartisan support. And while it could be a catalyst for lots of clean energy, it could also speed up polluting projects and limit oversight of new data centers. With data centers demanding more electricity for AI, environmental advocates fear that developers could take advantage of the reforms to evade public scrutiny and rely more heavily on fossil fuels. The bill sacrifices caution for speed, limiting environmental reviews and preventing communities from stopping a project from moving forward by taking it to court. “Whether it is permits to bulldoze wetlands, the fast-tracking of gas pipelines or general environmental review, with this legislation, data centers would not need to answer to the concerns of local communities,” Christy Goldfuss, executive director of the nonprofit Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC), says in an email to The Verge. “People would be shocked to realize their representatives are rushing such a consequential decision.” The sea change in Congress following the midterm elections could put the bill in an even more precarious position, giving Democrats a better shot at pushing for their priorities in the bill and potentially triggering a fight with President Donald Trump. Should it come up for a vote during the current lame-duck session or get kicked to next year, the bill will test whether Democrats and Republicans can actually get something done to address some of the biggest issues voters carried with them to the polls: rising energy costs and data centers encroaching on their communities. “They swung big with this bill. It’s a really good bipartisan compromise,” Xan Fishman, executive vice president of the Energy Program at the Bipartisan Policy Center, tells The Verge. Four senators calling themselves the “four corners” — Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Mike Lee (R-UT), and Martin Heinrich (D-NM) — introduced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) on September 30th. “If we can pass this bill, we will flood the grid with clean, affordable energy and make data centers start paying their fair share,” Whitehouse, a climate hawk, said in the press release. The announcement simultaneously garnered support from climate and renewable energy groups, as well as fossil fuel interests. “Pass the frickin’ bill so we can start building things again,” the US Oil & Gas Association said in a statement. The Senate could vote to move the bill forward as early as next week, teeing it up for potential passage before the end of the year, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center. Fishman expects President Trump will want to sign the bill if the current Republican-controlled Congress acts, adding in an email that the White House has been “very involved” in negotiations. Newly empowered Democrats, however, could decide to drag out debate on the bill until next year in order to make fewer concessions to Republicans. If it becomes law, the bill would limit the reach of bedrock laws (stemming back to the 1970s environmental movement) that protect water resources and endangered species and give the public an opportunity to weigh in on large projects that might impact public health. Over the years, however, reviews that once took months at most might take several years or even decades, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center. Fishman attributes the delays largely to lengthy legal battles. Now, agencies have to spend more time preparing for lawsuits as they consider permitting applications, Fishman says. That holds up development on all kinds of infrastructure projects, including cleaner energy alternatives to fossil fuels. Fishman expects BAAJA to be very effective in amending outdated permitting rules that have become burdensome to projects across the board, even those that might ultimately have a net positive impact on the environment. “Sometimes, bureaucratic processes that are created with good intentions kind of spiral out of control,” he says. “You want to protect the environment, you want to protect people, but you want to get to a yes or no [on a permit application] in a reasonable amount of time and you don’t want to have this endless litigation cycle.” The bill would set a 45-day deadline for a lead agency to issue a decision on a project after completing an environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). In many cases, NEPA review is the only opportunity for nearby residents to weigh in on large projects that involve the federal government. And it’s been a key tool for opponents to high-profile projects including the Dakota Access and Keystone XL pipelines. BAAJA narrows the scope of projects subject to NEPA, creating exclusions for transmission upgrades and certain pipeline expansions, to name a couple. Many projects receiving federal loans or grants or that have already been through a similar state environmental assessment would no longer trigger NEPA review. The bill also sets a strict new 150-day limit for anyone to challenge a project in court over alleged violations of NEPA, the Clean Water Act, Endangered Species Act, or National Historic Preservation Act. And BAAJA strips away a court’s ability to halt a project altogether even if it finds that a federal agency violated NEPA; it would simply force the agency to correct any issues. The Clean Water Act allows the Army Corps of Engineers to issue general permits to projects that discharge dredged material into US waters as long as they’re deemed as having “minimal adverse environmental effects.” BAAJA could make it easier for large projects including data centers to qualify for those permits. Some environmental groups are concerned that those general permits would take away public participation requirements for individual projects, especially when it comes to data centers that use a lot of water. The proposals in BAAJA amount to “rubber-stamping permits under the Clean Water Act” and “blocking interference from States and Tribes,” according to the environmental organization Earthjustice Action. They’re also concerned that BAAJA aligns with the Trump administration’s push to deregulate industry and weaken environmental protections in order to swiftly build out more data centers and fossil fuel infrastructure to power them. Data center energy demand has led to a surge of new gas projects in the US, and the bipartisan bill could help streamline reviews for new pipelines delivering fuel for data centers. “One very big reason why passing BAAJA is such a high priority for the gas industry is it will enable fast delivery of gas to fuel the data center build-out,” Earthjustice Action President Abigail Dillen said in a Thursday blog. “BAAJA delivers a precision strike for developers of dirty data centers.” Long pipeline delays slow data center development, according to energy research firm Wood Mackenzie. Permitting reform could benefit data center developers building out their own gas generation rather than relying solely on the grid, so-called “behind-the-meter” projects, by ending regulatory delays when it comes to connecting pipelines. Reforms would also speed grid-connected gas generation, Wood Mackenzie says in a recent news release. “I don’t think we’re seeing it as this bill helping one type of technology over the other. I think it clears the way for all technologies to get onto the grid a little quicker,” Siddhant Warrier, research analyst for North American Power for Wood Mackenzie, tells The Verge. Notably, the bill is supposed to protect bipartisan interests by preventing any single administration from attacking a particular project type — such as the Biden administration attempting to phase down oil and gas in the power sector or the Trump administration issuing stop work orders to wind farms. BAAJA aims to provide “project certainty” by barring federal agencies from canceling or suspending permits they’ve already approved in most cases. It even allows developers to take agencies to court for “disparate treatment” to sue for damages incurred from project delays. “This part of the legislation could also lead to a slew of industry lawsuits that result in taxpayers paying billions of dollars to private industry,” the NRDC warns in its analysis of the bill. It could also prevent communities from challenging projects, including data centers, that wind up having unforeseen consequences for the environment and public health. Despite those concerns, the NRDC and other advocacy groups are optimistic about the bill boosting renewable energy and enabling power grid upgrades needed to meet rising demand while keeping costs down. BAAJA could shorten the time needed to build a new transmission line nearly in half — from 10 years or more to around five or six years, the NRDC estimates. Transmission lines that carry electricity across long distances — key to getting electrons to urban centers from far-flung solar and wind farms — are particularly tricky to build because of the patchwork of permitting processes they’re subject to across different jurisdictions. Two separate reports project that the permitting bill would increase renewable energy capacity in the US and cut greenhouse gas emissions as a result. It also points to modest reductions in energy costs as a result of BAAJA passing compared to a baseline reflecting the status quo. The average annual cost of producing electricity would fall by as much as 7 percent by 2041, according to modeling by think tank Resources for the Future. Household electricity bills would lower by $50 to $78 per year by 2040, according to an analysis by research firm Rhodium Group. The White House put out its own analysis in October claiming that the average household could see their electricity bills fall by as much as $251 each year as a result of BAAJA. One of the ways BAAJA aims to keep utility bills from rising is to force data center developers to pay more for transmission costs. Current law prevents utilities from charging them for costs stemming from both new builds and existing infrastructure, which inadvertently shifts costs to other customers to fill in the gap. The bipartisan bill mandates what’s called “and pricing” so that data centers and other large electricity customers would be on the hook to pay for both added and existing infrastructure. The bill would also require utilities to disclose electricity sales to data centers. It would force large data center developers to make financial assurances to utilities before they break ground, as well as make them responsible for covering costs of new energy projects even if the data center shutters before the infrastructure is paid off. Unfortunately, the bill may only solve part of the problem since utility rates reflect more than just transmission costs. Increasing electricity demand from the data center boom can still raise prices for fuel and gas turbines, for example. And the bill doesn’t address other issues that have sparked backlash against data centers, like noise and air pollution from generators on site. Still, without permitting reform, gas and power prices would likely continue to climb as new energy projects keep hitting bottlenecks, according to Wood Mackenzie. Even environmental groups concerned about some of the provisions in BAAJA are holding out to see if Congress can amend the bill to strengthen environmental and consumer protections. The bill has become a sort of Rorschach test for its backers, one expert speaking on background tells The Verge. They’re all optimistic that their energy source of choice, be it oil and gas or solar and wind, will ultimately come out on top — as long as it gets the green light to build.

articles.title: Hundreds of Artex AI hacking tools found publicly exposed to the web | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Security researchers found hundreds of servers hosting the penetration testing tool Artex exposed to the internet, allowing anyone access to the hacking tool.
articles.body:
Security researchers have discovered hundreds of copies of a Chinese-made AI hacking tool publicly exposed to the internet for anyone to access, potentially allowing outsiders to launch cyberattacks against unsuspecting targets.

The hacking software, called Artex, is an open source autonomous penetration testing tool, meaning software that automatically probes computer systems for weaknesses, and it’s been linked to several cyberattacks since its public release in July. As open source software, it’s free for anyone to download and run on their own servers, making it a popular tool for those who cannot access Anthropic or OpenAI’s most advanced cybersecurity AI models for discovering security vulnerabilities. Microsoft has previously described Artex as a system of AI agents that can conduct cyberattacks “from reconnaissance through data exfiltration with little needed human interaction.”

In a blog post , cybersecurity firm Censys, which scans the internet for exposed or vulnerable systems, said that it identified more than 800 distinct deployments of Artex that were accessible from the web without needing a password to log in.

Silas Cutler, principal security researcher at Censys who wrote the blog post, said that not every instance of Artex is operated maliciously and many are used for authorized testers. But it’s unclear why hundreds of these Artex systems are exposed to the web, as the software does not require them to be accessible from the internet.

The findings underscore how even powerful hacking tools can be misconfigured to be publicly accessible by anyone, increasing the chance that someone will find and misuse them. The publicly accessible systems also expose attack tools, such as implants (hidden malicious software) used to compromise and maintain persistent access to a victim’s network.

Security companies have linked the use of Artex to several broad-scale cyberattacks, including against the Korean finance industry in September . Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike attributed the attacks to a Chinese-speaking hacker who used an Artex instance in the attacks, in part because the hacker had left an “open directory” hosting the system. Censys said that its data showed the Artex instance in question had been publicly exposed for months, and appeared to contain more attack data that extended “well beyond South Korean banks,” including payment and gaming companies.

Artex was also used in an attack on IT support giant ConnectWise earlier in October , which allowed Chinese-linked hackers to spy on thousands of organizations whose data and files are hosted in Microsoft’s cloud. Microsoft, which has visibility into the attack, said in a blog post that the hackers used Artex to break into customers’ cloud environments and steal their data at such speed that defenders had “little time to detect and respond.”

Many of the attacks linked to Artex involved exploiting simple vulnerabilities, such as guessing weak or known passwords, and a lack of multi-factor authentication.

The findings show that simple vulnerabilities, including misconfigurations, can expose both the attacker and their targets.

Artex has since announced it would go closed-source, effectively limiting further releases for paid customers. There are still dozens of copies of Artex’s code available on code-sharing sites that can still be used in active attacks.

articles.title: Homeland Security data leak exposes 41K workers
articles.summary: A massive DHS data leak exposed records of over 41,000 employees, revealing links to undercover ICE operations, Palantir tools and AI platforms.
articles.body: You might think an employee directory sounds pretty harmless. After all, most workplaces keep lists of names and phone numbers so people can reach one another. But what happens when that information belongs to thousands of federal agents, including people connected to undercover investigations? A massive Homeland Security data leak has exposed records involving more than 41,000 employees and contractors. The information includes contact details, office locations and internal access groups tied to sensitive government operations. Some records even point to surveillance programs and artificial intelligence tools used within the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). Now, federal officials are scrambling to contain the fallout as concerns grow over the safety of agents and their families. And there's a bigger cybersecurity lesson here that applies well beyond Washington. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. DHS INVESTIGATES MASSIVE DATA BREACH EXPOSING 40,000 EMPLOYEES, INCLUDING ICE AND BORDER PATROL AGENTS What the Homeland Security data leak exposed On Oct. 28, the nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets published a collection of DHS records under the name Icepick. The information reportedly came from a group calling itself the Department of Peace, which claims it obtained access to internal government systems. The records reportedly cover DHS and seven of its component agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP). The files contain employee names, agency email addresses and workplace locations. They also include phone numbers, some identified as cell phone numbers, along with supervisors and internal access-group memberships. However, it has not been established that employees' private home addresses were included. CBP accounts for more than half the records, while roughly 10,000 involve ICE. Another 6,200 are tied to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. The records were last updated on Aug. 19, so some assignments may have changed. That's an enormous amount of organizational information to have floating around publicly. And the deeper researchers looked, the more sensitive the findings became. Undercover ICE operations appear in leaked records One of the most alarming findings involves internal groups associated with undercover investigations. WIRED identified 39 Homeland Security Investigations employees connected to access groups referencing certified undercover operations. Other groups reference communications interception programs and surveillance technology. The files also reveal reporting relationships that could help someone understand how different parts of DHS work together. That raises a difficult security concern. People conducting undercover investigations depend on keeping certain relationships and assignments confidential. Revealing those connections could create risks for ongoing operations. Still, membership in an internal access group does not automatically confirm that every person listed was working undercover. The leaked records offer clues about sensitive assignments, but they don't establish every individual's operational role. Former acting ICE director John Sandweg called the exposure a "nightmare scenario". He warned that revealing agents' identities could put people in danger and interfere with criminal investigations. Why Palantir and Grok appear in the DHS leak Here's another part of this story that caught my attention. The leaked records reveal internal access groups referencing technology used for investigations and government operations. Some groups mention Palantir's Falcon investigative platform, which helps investigators analyze information. Others reference surveillance-related software, including tools used to examine phone records. Then there's artificial intelligence. WIRED found groups mentioning OpenAI's ChatGPT, Google's Gemini and Microsoft's Copilot. One group labeled "Grok.com" included eight DHS technology officials. That doesn't prove these employees actively used the services or that the technology companies experienced breaches. The group names can reflect access permissions rather than actual activity. Even so, the information offers outsiders a closer look at the technologies DHS personnel may have access to. For an agency responsible for national security, those internal details can be valuable to people looking for weaknesses. FBI SAYS SOURCE OF ITS JOBS PORTAL BREACH STILL UNKNOWN AS HACKERS ALLEGE EMPLOYEE DATA COMPROMISED How did hackers get access to Homeland Security records? The group claiming responsibility says it accessed the information through DHS's Okta sign-in system. Okta provides identity and access-management technology that organizations use to control employee logins. However, Okta says it has no evidence that its own systems or data were compromised. That leaves the actual entry point unresolved. DHS has acknowledged a potential breach and says it is investigating. The department has not publicly confirmed how the information was obtained. It's also important to understand what has been established so far. The reporting centers on personnel information and access-group details. It has not confirmed that employee passwords, intercepted communications or investigative case files were included. Until investigators explain what happened, there's no reliable basis for blaming a specific vulnerability or software provider. We reached out to the Department of Homeland Security and Okta for additional comment. A DHS spokesperson provided the following statement: "DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively. We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available." Okta had not responded to our request for additional comment by our deadline. DHS tries to remove leaked employee information As the records spread online, DHS moved to limit access. On Oct. 29, a company reportedly authorized to seek content removals on behalf of ICE contacted Icelandic hosting provider FlokiNET. The request warned that the database exposed more than 40,000 identifiable individuals to potential harassment and physical harm. However, the hosting company declined to remove the material, saying the records contained workplace contact information rather than private home contact details. The database briefly became inaccessible before appearing again elsewhere. Then, on Oct. 30, SITE Intelligence Group had reportedly identified threatening online rhetoric following the release. Some social media users reportedly threatened immigration officers and their families. Those reports raise additional concerns about what happens after sensitive personnel information becomes searchable. Even if the original files disappear, copies may already exist elsewhere. Why this data leak should concern people outside government You might be wondering why a federal employee database should concern someone who works in an office, owns a small business or has nothing to do with immigration enforcement. Think about how a convincing scam works. Someone contacts you claiming to be from your company's IT department. They know your supervisor's name and your work email address. They even mention an internal system you're familiar with. Suddenly, that unexpected message sounds a lot more believable. That's the danger when attackers combine workplace records with information they find elsewhere online. They can use those details to create personalized phishing messages or impersonate trusted colleagues. We've seen related concerns before. In our reporting on the FBI hack claim involving sensitive personnel data, we examined how employee information could expose individuals and their families to additional risks. And that's what concerns me about this latest incident. Even information that seems routine can become dangerous when someone connects it to other records. Tips to protect yourself from workplace data leaks You may have no control over how your employer stores its records. However, there are ways to reduce the amount of personal information available about you and make targeted scams harder to pull off. 1) Verify unexpected emails and calls If someone contacts you claiming to be from your employer's IT department, don't assume they're legitimate because they know your name or job title. Contact your IT department using a phone number or communication channel you already trust. Avoid clicking links in unexpected password-reset emails, especially when the message creates urgency. A convincing message can still lead to a fake login page designed to steal your credentials. 2) Strengthen your passwords and account security Your primary email account deserves special attention because criminals may use it to reset passwords for other services. Use a strong, unique password for every important account and consider a reputable password manager to create and store them. Turn on multifactor authentication or passkeys wherever available. Also review your recovery email addresses and phone numbers to make sure nobody has changed them without your permission. 3) Use strong antivirus software Once criminals have detailed information about you, they may send phishing messages containing malicious links or infected attachments. Strong antivirus software can provide an additional layer of protection by helping detect malicious downloads, known phishing websites and malware before they cause damage. Keep your operating system and security software updated so you receive the latest protections. Antivirus software cannot remove your information from a leaked database. However, it can help protect your devices against attacks that may follow an exposure. No security tool catches every threat, so continue checking unexpected messages carefully. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com. 4) Use a data removal service to reduce your exposure Here's something I strongly recommend considering. Data brokers collect personal information from public records and online sources. That information can include your home address, personal phone number and details about relatives. When someone already has your workplace information, finding additional personal details may make harassment or impersonation attempts easier. A reputable data removal service can help remove your personal information from participating data broker and people-search websites. Services such as Incogni automate removal requests and continue checking for information that reappears. You can also contact individual data brokers yourself, although that takes more time and ongoing follow-up. Keep in mind that these services cannot guarantee removal from every website or erase the original DHS leak. For more information, see our guide on how to remove your personal information from the web and keep it from coming back. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com. 5) Review what strangers can find about you online Search your own name and see what appears. You may discover old professional profiles, forgotten social media accounts or websites showing personal contact details. Check the privacy settings on your social media accounts and limit how much information strangers can see about your family. Be especially careful about publicly revealing your home location or daily routine if you work in a sensitive position. If you discover unwanted personal information online, contact the website or platform and request removal where possible. 6) Watch for identity theft and unusual account activity The reported DHS records center on workplace information. So far, there has been no confirmation that Social Security numbers or financial account details were included. Still, exposed contact information can help criminals build more convincing scams. Monitor your important accounts for unfamiliar activity and pay attention to suspicious password-reset messages. If you discover that sensitive identity information has been compromised elsewhere, consider freezing your credit with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. Identity monitoring services may also help flag certain signs of fraud. However, they cannot prevent every type of identity theft or guarantee that your information will stay private. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at CyberGuy.com. 7) Report suspicious activity and threats immediately If someone uses your workplace information to impersonate a colleague or threaten you, document what happened. Save relevant emails, screenshots and messages, then report the incident to your employer's security team. If you receive threats of violence, contact law enforcement. You can also report suspected internet crime through the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov/. If you're an employee whose information may be involved in a breach, ask your employer whether you were affected and what protective steps it recommends. Don't rely on unsolicited callers claiming they can verify your exposure. Kurt's key takeaways What strikes me about this Homeland Security leak is how much damage a collection of workplace records could potentially cause. We're talking about information that many organizations use every day to help employees do their jobs. Yet in the wrong hands, those same details can help identify people involved in sensitive operations or make targeted scams much more convincing. I also believe there's an important conversation to be had about government transparency. Americans have a right to question how federal agencies operate and how officers are held accountable. But I worry about the consequences when information tied to undercover personnel becomes publicly searchable, especially now that threats against employees and their families have been reported. For me, the biggest unanswered question is how DHS allowed this information to become exposed in the first place. The department needs to explain what happened and how it plans to prevent another incident. In the meantime, there's a lesson here for all of us. Pay attention to how much personal information is available about you online. You may never be able to remove everything, but reducing your exposure can make it harder for someone to target you. Do you believe exposing the identities of federal agents is justified in the name of government transparency, even when it could put undercover operations and employees' families at risk? articles.title: DOJ, Fed’s Cook Seek Pause in Court Fight Over Trump Firing Push
articles.summary: Lawyers for the US Justice Department and Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook asked a federal judge to keep the legal battle over President Donald Trump’s bid...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Lawyers for the US Justice Department and Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook asked a federal judge to keep the legal battle over President Donald Trump's bid to fire her on hold pending a White House hearing set for next month.

Legal teams for DOJ and Cook filed a brief, joint report on Friday to US District Judge Jia Cobb saying the court should pause upcoming deadlines and that they'd come back to her with another update in early January.

The US Supreme Court ruled this summer that Trump failed to give Cook a legitimate opportunity to defend herself before initially trying to fire her last year. The justices allowed Cook to stay in her post for now, sending the case back to Cobb. In August, Trump revived the effort to oust her.

Trump convened a White House committee to investigate whether he has "cause" to remove her — specifically digging into unproven mortgage-fraud allegations against Cook that he relied on in trying to fire her the first time. The panel is set to meet Dec. 14, according to a White House official.

Cook and the White House are discussing the "specifics and details" for how Trump's "committee of inquiry" will proceed, the lawyers wrote in Friday's filing.

Cook has denied wrongdoing and accused Trump of trying to remove her in order to undermine the central bank's longstanding independence. Trump has lashed out at Cook and former Chair Jerome Powell for resisting his calls to cut interest rates.

The Supreme Court didn't directly rule on whether Trump eventually could fire Cook, focusing instead on the due process issue. But Chief Justice John Roberts included strong language in the court's opinion stressing the importance of the Fed's distance from political influence and laying out criteria for when it would be permissible for a president to remove a governor for "cause."

There's been no action in the case in the months that followed. Cobb, presiding in federal court in Washington is likely to keep the proceedings frozen as long as the government and Cook agree that's the best course of action.

Fed officials voted Oct. 28 to hold interest rates steady, though Cook was one of two officials who dissented, preferring instead to raise borrowing costs to help curb inflation. Policymakers are set to meet again Dec. 8-9, when investors expect they will lift rates for the second time this year.

articles.standfirst: Especialistas ouvidos pela reportagem analisam padrão relatado por mulheres que denunciaram homem de Sertãozinho (SP) por suspeita de golpe. Prejuízos chegam a R$ 30 mil.
articles.summary: Psicóloga e criminalista analisam padrão relatado por mulheres que denunciaram homem de Sertãozinho (SP). Pelo menos cinco procuraram a polícia; prejuízos chegam a R$ 30 mil.
articles.body:
Pelo menos cinco mulheres procuraram a polícia para denunciar Fernando Vasco Fernandes, de 38 anos, de Sertãozinho (SP), por suspeita de estelionato. Segundo elas, ele iniciava relacionamentos por aplicativos de namoro, passava a pedir dinheiro e não devolvia os valores.

Em dois dos casos, as vítimas relataram prejuízos de R$ 26 mil e R$ 30 mil. À EPTV , afiliada da TV Globo, elas explicaram que os relacionamentos começaram com demonstrações de carinho, elogios e planos de casamento e de ter filhos e depois vinham pedidos de dinheiro, promessas de pagamento e ameaças durante as cobranças.

Para a psicóloga Dariene Castellucci, esse tipo de golpe explora necessidades comuns a qualquer pessoa, como o desejo de ser amada, reconhecida e de construir uma relação de confiança.

De acordo com a especialista, a situação não está relacionada à inteligência ou ao grau de instrução das vítimas.

"Esses golpistas se valem de necessidades legítimas humanas, como ser amado, pertencer, ser reconhecido e construir relações de confiança. Eles fazem esse mapeamento e entendem aquilo que faz sentido para cada mulher."

Na legislação brasileira, o chamado estelionato sentimental não é um crime específico, mas a conduta pode ser enquadrada como estelionato, dependendo das provas reunidas. A pena prevista é de um a cinco anos de prisão e multa. (entenda abaixo) .

Fernando não foi localizado para comentar as acusações. A EPTV , afiliada da TV Globo, esteve em um endereço ligado a ele em Sertãozinho , mas não o encontrou. Nenhum advogado que o represente foi localizado até a última atualização desta reportagem.

Fernando Vasco Fernandes, de Sertãozinho (SP), denunciado por suposto golpe contra mulheres — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

Segundo Dariene, quem aplica esse tipo de golpe observa os desejos, as fragilidades e as expectativas de cada pessoa antes de construir uma relação aparentemente próxima.

A psicóloga afirma que o afeto passa a ser utilizado como instrumento de manipulação: a vítima acredita que está ajudando alguém com quem mantém uma relação e que o dinheiro será devolvido.

"Isso não está vinculado à capacidade de pensar, de raciocinar ou ao nível de instrução. Todos nós temos essas necessidades e o desejo de sermos amados. Eles se valem do sentimento para manipular e controlar essas mulheres."

Uma das denunciantes, moradora de Ribeirão Preto (SP), afirmou que sentia vergonha de contar à família o que havia acontecido. Ela diz ter transferido cerca de R$ 13 mil por Pix e comprado um iPhone de aproximadamente R$ 13 mil, parcelado em 20 vezes, depois que Fernando se comprometeu a pagar as prestações.

Com dívidas, a mulher disse que recorreu a agiotas e chegou a tentar tirar a própria vida. Depois de receber ajuda de uma amiga, procurou a polícia.

Dariene reforça que esse tipo de manipulação pode atingir qualquer pessoa e não deve ser atribuído à falta de inteligência da vítima.

"Isso vale para qualquer pessoa, para mim, para você, para essas mulheres. Não está vinculado à capacidade de pensar, de raciocinar ou ao nível de instrução."

Em troca de mensagens, engenheiro pede que seja deixado em paz ao ser cobrado por pagamento de iPhone Sertãozinho, SP — Foto: Reprodução/EPTV

Demonstrações exageradas de carinho logo no início da relação, intimidade construída rapidamente e planos para casamento ou filhos estão entre os comportamentos que exigem atenção, segundo a psicóloga.

"Constrói-se uma intimidade muito rápida e, principalmente, planos de um futuro junto. Intimidade e confiança, não apenas nas relações amorosas, são construídas a longo prazo. Tudo aquilo que é muito intenso de imediato já é um sinal de alerta."

Nos relatos apresentados à polícia, as mulheres afirmam que Fernando se apresentava como engenheiro agrônomo e fazendeiro. Ele alegava problemas como roubo, bloqueio de contas bancárias e falta de dinheiro para liberar produtos.

Uma das denunciantes guardou áudios em que ele a chamava de "amor" enquanto pedia valores entre R$ 250 e R$ 2 mil. Segundo ela, os pedidos eram acompanhados da promessa de que o dinheiro seria devolvido.

Dariene afirma que uma relação saudável precisa permitir recusas sem pressão, ameaças ou mudanças de comportamento.

"Responsabilizar-se financeiramente por alguém não é uma demonstração de afeto. Uma relação saudável se estabelece com limites, com espaço para dizer não e, principalmente, com a nossa autonomia preservada."

O estelionato sentimental não aparece com esse nome no Código Penal. Segundo o advogado criminalista Leonardo Pontes, estes casos podem ser enquadrados no artigo 171, quando há obtenção de vantagem ilícita, prejuízo à vítima e uso de fraude para induzi-la ou mantê-la em erro.

"Não temos na legislação brasileira um tipo penal específico denominado estelionato sentimental. O enquadramento pode ocorrer no artigo 171 do Código Penal quando alguém obtém vantagem ilícita em prejuízo da vítima por meio de uma relação amorosa ou de confiança."

A pena prevista para o estelionato é de um a cinco anos de prisão e multa. Na fraude eletrônica, ela varia de quatro a oito anos, também com multa.

O enquadramento na modalidade eletrônica depende da maneira como o crime foi praticado . O simples fato de duas pessoas terem se conhecido por um aplicativo de namoro não define automaticamente a fraude eletrônica.

O Código Penal prevê essa modalidade quando informações da vítima ou de terceiros são obtidas por meio de redes sociais, ligações, e-mails, aplicativos ou outros meios fraudulentos semelhantes.

A pena ainda pode ser aumentada se o criminoso utilizar servidor mantido fora do Brasil ou se a vítima for idosa ou considerada vulnerável.

Desde maio de 2026, também não é mais necessária uma manifestação formal da vítima para que o Ministério Público possa apresentar denúncia por estelionato. A mudança ocorreu depois que a Lei 15.397 revogou o trecho do Código Penal que condicionava o processo à representação.

"Antes de maio, a vítima precisava representar contra quem praticou o estelionato. Com a mudança na lei, essa representação deixou de ser necessária, e o Ministério Público pode denunciar se entender que existem elementos", afirma o advogado.

Transferência voluntária não afasta fraude

Em uma decisão na esfera cível, de 2025, o Superior Tribunal de Justiça (STJ) entendeu que o fato de a vítima entregar o dinheiro voluntariamente não afasta a ilicitude quando a transferência é resultado de uma fraude.

Naquele caso, um homem havia simulado um relacionamento amoroso e convencido uma mulher a contrair empréstimos em benefício dele. Segundo o tribunal, a ilusão criada foi determinante para que ela entregasse o dinheiro.

"A essência do golpe está justamente na ilusão criada. A vítima paga voluntariamente porque foi enganada. Dizer que ela transferiu ou entregou o dinheiro porque quis não afasta, por si só, a fraude", explica Pontes.

A decisão também diferencia os gastos comuns de um relacionamento das despesas provocadas pela fraude. Presentes, jantares e viagens, por exemplo, não geram automaticamente direito à devolução.

Já empréstimos, dívidas, compras e outras despesas extraordinárias feitas em benefício exclusivo da outra pessoa podem resultar em indenização por danos materiais e morais, desde que a fraude seja comprovada.

Além da investigação criminal, a vítima pode recorrer à Justiça na tentativa de recuperar o dinheiro e pedir indenização.

Para isso, Leonardo Pontes diz que é importante preservar os registros da relação e das movimentações financeiras.

"Conversas de WhatsApp, transferências bancárias e mensagens por outros aplicativos são muito importantes para que a ação tenha uma sustentação sólida e possa viabilizar o ressarcimento", afirma o criminalista.

Entre as provas que podem ser apresentadas estão:

Conversas e áudios enviados por aplicativos;

Comprovantes de transferências e pagamentos;

Faturas de cartão e contratos de empréstimos;

Fotografias e informações dos perfis utilizados;

Registros de cobranças e eventuais ameaças.

Segundo as denunciantes, Fernando mudava de comportamento quando era cobrado . Uma mulher afirma que ele passou a ser grosseiro e fez menção a um suposto policial para intimidá-la.

Outra apresentou um áudio em que o homem diz que não seria preso por ter formação superior e que não devolveria o dinheiro. O g1 não conseguiu confirmar de forma independente que a voz na gravação é de Fernando.

Os relatos e os materiais reunidos pelas mulheres foram encaminhados à Polícia Civil. As circunstâncias de cada caso ainda são apuradas.

articles.title: Conheça túnel natural em meio ao manguezal que atrai turistas no litoral do Ceará | G1
articles.standfirst: Passagem cercada por vegetação fica às margens do Rio Aracatiaçu, em Amontada, e pode ser visitada em passeios de barco.
articles.summary: Passagem cercada por vegetação fica às margens do Rio Aracatiaçu, em Amontada, e pode ser visitada em passeios de barco.
articles.body:
Um caminho cercado pelo verde do manguezal, onde a vegetação forma um arco sobre os visitantes. Assim é o Túnel do Amor , em Moitas , no litoral oeste do Ceará.

Localizada a cerca de 220km de Fortaleza , a Praia de Moitas é um vilarejo de pescadores localizado no município de Amontada . O famoso túnel fica às margens do Rio Aracatiaçu, em um estuário, onde as águas do rio se encontram com as do mar, e se tornou um dos principais atrativos turísticos da região.

Praia de Moitas em Amontada. — Foto: Helene Santos/Divulgação

Nas redes sociais, a atração ganhou o apelido de "túnel do amor", mas a população nativa a conhece por outro nome: camboa .

🌊 Entenda: O termo "camboa" é usado para se referir a um canal natural de água que enche e seca com o ritmo das marés, exatamente como acontece no "túnel".

🎣A palavra também dá nome a uma forma ancestral de pesca artesanal: a criação de pequenos lagos artificiais, covas ou cercados de pedra à beira-mar para capturar peixes que entram na maré alta e ficam retidos no refluxo da maré baixa.

Embora os visitantes costumem falar no singular, a geografia do local reserva mais de uma surpresa: existem, na verdade, dois túneis de manguezal na região . O principal e mais famoso possui cerca de 400 metros de extensão. Já o segundo túnel tem aproximadamente 300 metros.

Adriano Souza , de 27 anos, mora há 50 metros do Rio Aracatiaçu e é um dos barqueiros que conduz os visitantes pelo labirinto natural. Natural de Amontada, ele navega pelas águas do Aracatiaçu desde os 14, acompanhando de perto a transformação da região em rota turística.

"A principal fonte do passeio, o mais chamativo, é o Túnel do Amor. Esse nome foram os turistas que deram, mas a gente, nativo daqui de Moitas, conhece como Camboa. É nome de pescador, que vem dos nossos pais, avós e bisavós", destaca Adriano.

Os passeios podem ser feitos em grupo, quando o visitante compartilha o barco com outros turistas, ou de forma privativa. Na modalidade compartilhada, o valor é a partir de R$ 50 por pessoa, com duração aproximada de 40 minutos.

Esses túneis naturais têm explicação na botânica . Segundo a pesquisadora, doutora e líder do Laboratório de Ecologia de Manguezais (Ecomangue/IFCE), Rafaela Camargo Maia, a formação da galeria é um processo biológico gradual .

Ela explica que o crescimento dos troncos e a expansão lateral dos galhos nas duas margens do canal fazem com que as copas das árvores se encontrem sobre a água, criando uma cobertura vegetal contínua. Esse teto natural bloqueia a luz solar direta, formando as áreas sombreadas do percurso, enquanto o sistema de raízes garante a fixação das árvores no solo lodoso.

Em Amontada, o estuário reúne diferentes paisagens naturais, como manguezais, praias e outros ambientes costeiros, que favorecem a diversidade de espécies da fauna e da flora. Todo o manguezal é protegido como Área de Preservação Permanente (APP) pelo Código Florestal Brasileiro (Lei nº 12.651/2012) devido a sua extrema fragilidade.

A vegetação é típica do litoral cearense, marcada pelo mangue-vermelho ( Rhizophora mangle ), mangue-branco ( Laguncularia racemosa ) e mangue-preto ( Avicennia schaueriana ), além de áreas de restinga nas dunas vizinhas.

Essa estrutura funciona como o principal " berçário natural " da vida marinha na região. A dinâmica das marés renova os nutrientes e cria um ambiente protegido para a reprodução e alimentação de invertebrados e peixes.

Entre as espécies que dependem diretamente do estuário do Aracatiaçu estão:

🦀 Crustáceos: caranguejo-uçá, aratu, guaiamum, siris e camarões;

🐡 Peixes: baiacus, carapebas, carapitus, camurins (robalo) e tainhas;

🕊️ Aves costeiras: garça-branca-pequena e garça-azul.

Fonte de renda e alimento para a comunidade local

Passeio para o Túnel do Amor é um dos mais buscados em Amontada. — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

Além da importância ambiental, o manguezal também está diretamente ligado à economia e à cultura das comunidades que vivem às margens do rio. Em localidades como Moitas, os passeios turísticos conduzidos pelos próprios moradores são uma alternativa de geração de renda e uma forma de valorizar os conhecimentos tradicionais sobre o território.

Para Rafaela, a conservação do mangueza l está diretamente relacionada à segurança alimentar , à geração de renda e à preservação dos modos de vida das comunidades tradicionais de Amontada.

Túnel do Amor em rio no Ceará tem passagem 'secreta', atrai casais e bomba nas redes — Foto: Cadastur/Divulgação

O trajeto de Fortaleza até o município de Amontada pode ser feito de carro ou ônibus. É importante ter em mente que o Túnel do Rio Aracatiaçu fica próximo à praia de Moitas e leva aproximadamente 1 hora do centro de Amontada até o local.

Para chegar até o ponto de partida do passeio de barco, é preciso se deslocar até o Porto da Barra de Moitas ou contratar um passeio de buggy até o local.

Infográfico: Túnel natural atrai turistas a manguezal no Ceará — Foto: Arte/g1

Muitos turistas também optam pelo passeio de buggy pelo lado oeste da Praia de Moitas. Além do passeio de barco pelo Rio Aracatiaçu, o roteiro inclui paradas na Ilha das Ostras, na Lagoa da Cobra e na Duna do Pôr do Sol. O g1 lista os principais pontos recomendados pelas empresas de turismo da região:

Túnel Canoé: Um corredor formado por plantas e flores, por onde normalmente passam os passeios de buggy;

Lençóis cearenses: Piscinas naturais que se formam entre as dunas da região;

Encontro do rio com o mar: Um belo espetáculo natural onde as águas do Rio Aracatiaçu se encontram com o mar;

Ilha das Ostras: Localizada às margens do Rio Aracatiaçu, essa ilha pode ser acessada de barco ou por veículos 4x4 e buggies pelas dunas. A principal atração é a degustação de ostras frescas, diretamente no local;

Lagoa das Cobras: Apesar do nome, não há cobras de verdade por ali, apenas esculturas decorativas. Localizada em Moitas, a lagoa tem águas calmas, ideais para um banho tranquilo.

articles.body:
DC officials ask incoming Democratic governors to pull Guard troops

Washington, D.C., officials are calling on incoming Democratic governors in five states that flipped blue to recall their National Guard troops from the nation’s capital.

During a D.C. Council hearing on Thursday, council member Brooke Pinto (D) — the chair of the public safety committee — said she would soon send a letter on behalf of the council to ask the governors-elect in Iowa , Georgia, Nevada, Ohio and Texas to “immediately” withdraw their soldiers back to their states.

“It’s something they can do their first day in office,” she said.

“While we have asked all of the governors across the country in the past to pull back their troops, we’ve been met with a lot of resistance and a lot of governors who are following the lead from President Trump,” Pinto noted. “But we now have the opportunity , with Tuesday’s election results, to turn the tide of what we’re seeing in Washington, D.C., and to have some real accountability to the federal government.”

Some 3,100 National Guard troops are deployed in Washington as part of President Trump’s “Making the District of Columbia Safe and Beautiful” mission, which was announced last summer.

Of that number, just fewer than 760 troops are part of the D.C. National Guard — which is controlled by the sitting president — and 2,341 have been sent to the city by states and territories, nearly all of which are currently controlled by Republican governors, according to the mission’s joint task force .

While Texas, Ohio and Nevada currently only have one or two guard troops sent from each of their states, Georgia and Iowa can make a far bigger dent if they pull their 514 and 110 troops, respectively.

Should Alaska also flip to a Democratic governor — the race has yet to be called but has former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins (D) currently leading — it would mean an additional 34 guard members could be recalled.

That means a total of 662 troops could be recalled from D.C. on come January.
