articles.title: Is someone already using your identity? Check these 8 places
articles.summary: Identity theft can hide in phone accounts, medical records and utility bills long before it shows on a credit report. Eight places to check now.
articles.body: When people think about identity theft, they often start with a credit report or bank statement. Those are important places to look, but they are not the only ones. Someone using your identity may be trying to open a phone line, start utility service, use medical benefits or create a payment plan that never appears on your usual accounts. The warning signs of identity theft can be easy to miss, especially when fraudulent activity happens outside your primary financial accounts. You do not need to investigate every record today. Start with these eight places, focusing first on accounts that could cause the most damage. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. SOMEONE COULD HAVE OPENED AN ACCOUNT IN YOUR NAME. CHECK NOW 1. Bank accounts, credit cards and payment apps Review checking, savings, credit card, investment, retirement and payment-app activity for transactions you do not recognize. Look beyond purchases. A new external bank connection, authorized user, payment method, mailing address or phone number can also signal an unauthorized account change. Turn on transaction and security alerts wherever your financial institution offers them. If you find an unfamiliar transaction, contact the institution through its official website or the number on your statement. Do not use a number from a suspicious text or email. 2. Credit reports and new inquiries Check all three major credit reports for accounts, hard inquiries, collections, addresses or employers you do not recognize. A fraudulent credit card, personal loan or retail-financing account may appear here even when your checking account looks normal. Use AnnualCreditReport.com to access your reports. You can currently request free online credit reports from Equifax, Experian and TransUnion once a week. An unfamiliar entry does not automatically mean fraud. Some lenders operate under different business names. Verify questionable information with the company before disputing it. Pro tip: Consider freezing your credit with all three bureaus. Credit freezes are free, do not affect your credit score and can make it harder for someone to open new credit accounts in your name. 3. Buy now, pay later and retail accounts Buy now, pay later services and store-financing accounts can be easy to overlook because they may not feel like traditional credit cards. Check services you have used for unfamiliar orders, payment plans, saved addresses or account-opening messages. Some buy now, pay later loans may not appear on your traditional credit reports. Reporting practices vary by provider and loan type. Search your inbox for purchase confirmations, shipping notices and payment reminders you did not expect. Open the retailer's official app or type its web address yourself rather than clicking a link in an unexpected message. 4. Phone and mobile-carrier accounts Your phone number can provide access to other accounts because it may receive verification codes and password-reset messages. Review your carrier account for unfamiliar devices, lines, eSIMs, upgrades, address changes or changes to your account PIN. A sudden loss of cellular service can be an early warning sign of a SIM swap, although outages and equipment problems can have other explanations. Contact your carrier through an official channel if the change is unexpected. Pro tip: Ask your carrier about account PINs, port-out protection and SIM-swap security features. These safeguards may help prevent someone from transferring your number without authorization. 5. Utilities and household services Review electric, gas, water, internet and other household-service accounts. Someone using your name or personal information may try to start service, change an account or leave an unpaid balance behind. Utility fraud may not appear on your credit report immediately. A bill, welcome email, service appointment or shutoff notice for an account you did not request is worth investigating. You can also request a report from the National Consumer Telecom & Utilities Exchange (NCTUE). This specialty reporting service collects information from participating phone, pay-TV and utility companies. You are entitled to one free NCTUE report every 12 months upon request. It may reveal accounts or service requests missing from your traditional credit reports, although it does not cover every provider. If you find an unfamiliar account, note the date, address and service details. Then contact the company and ask which information was used to open or change the account. 6. Medical and insurance records Look for explanations of benefits, medical bills, prescription notices or insurance communications related to care you did not receive. Medical identity theft can create an unexpected bill, but it can also place incorrect information in your medical record. For example, someone may use your insurance information to obtain treatment, leaving behind records that could affect future care or insurance claims. If something looks unfamiliar, contact the provider or insurer directly and ask for the records connected to the claim. Do not ignore a small bill simply because the amount seems insignificant. The inaccurate medical information may be a bigger concern. 7. Government, tax and employment records Watch for notices from the IRS, Social Security Administration or a state benefits agency that do not match your situation. Examples include income reported by an unfamiliar employer, a tax return you did not file or unemployment benefits claimed in your name. You can review tax information through your IRS online account. You can also check your earnings history through your "my Social Security" account. If you notice unfamiliar earnings, contact the Social Security Administration about correcting your record. Pro tip: Consider requesting an IRS Identity Protection PIN. This free, six-digit number helps prevent someone else from filing a federal tax return using your Social Security number. You can learn more at IRS.gov. Always use official government websites to review or report suspicious activity. If an unexpected message claims to come from an agency, do not follow its links. Find the agency's website independently. 8. Email, social accounts and recovery settings Your email and social accounts may not show a financial loss, but they can reveal whether someone is trying to take over your digital identity. Review recent sign-ins, sent messages, forwarding rules, recovery addresses, trusted devices and connected apps. Email deserves special attention because someone with access to your inbox may be able to reset passwords for other accounts. If you see unfamiliar access, change your password from a trusted device, sign out unfamiliar sessions and enable stronger multifactor authentication. Where available, use an authenticator app, passkey or security key rather than relying only on text-message verification codes. IDENTITY RESTORATION: WHAT TO DO AFTER IDENTITY THEFT How to check without making it a full-time job Spread the review across four short sessions: If nothing looks unusual, record the date of your review. The goal is to recognize unfamiliar activity, not question every legitimate bill. However, do not wait for a scheduled review if you receive a suspicious account alert or discover a potentially fraudulent transaction. Investigate those warnings immediately. How to tell whether an alert deserves attention An unfamiliar message does not always mean identity theft. A lender may use a business name you do not recognize, a family member may have used a shared device or a service provider may have changed its billing name. Look for related warning signs. A new account combined with an unfamiliar address, phone change or collection notice deserves immediate attention. Even a single unauthorized transaction or account opening warrants investigation. When you are unsure, compare the record with your own statements and contact the company to explain the mismatch. Do not confirm sensitive personal details to an unexpected caller. Contact the company yourself using a verified number. What to save when you find something unusual Keep the original bill, email or letter, but do not click links inside an unexpected message. Write down the date, company name, account or service involved and the first sign that something was wrong. If you call, record the department, case number and follow-up date. For credit issues, save relevant copies of all three reports. For phone, bank or email issues, keep account-change notices and screenshots. Store these records securely so you can refer to them when speaking with the company, a credit bureau or an identity theft recovery specialist. If the account is old or the name looks unfamiliar Do not assume an unfamiliar record is fraudulent simply because you do not recognize the company name. A lender, utility provider or collection agency may use a parent-company name. Contact the organization using verified contact information. Ask for the date the account was opened, the address associated with it and the steps required to confirm whether it belongs to you. If the company confirms the account is fraudulent, ask for a fraud case number and written instructions. Then add the issue to your records and check whether related activity appears elsewhere. How identity monitoring can help protect against identity theft Checking your accounts regularly is a smart first step, but identity theft can happen between reviews. Identity monitoring tools can help by watching for certain changes involving your personal information and alerting you when something suspicious appears. Some services monitor credit activity, financial accounts, personal information found in data breaches and certain types of account openings. Depending on the service, you may receive alerts about unfamiliar credit inquiries, changes to your personal information or possible misuse of your identity. What to look for in identity monitoring services Not all identity monitoring services offer the same protection. Before signing up, consider these features: One advantage of using an identity monitoring service is having someone keeping watch for suspicious activity even when you are not actively checking your accounts. Depending on the provider and plan, these services can monitor multiple sources of information and send alerts when something needs your attention. Some also provide dedicated restoration specialists who can help guide you through the recovery process if your identity is stolen. A paid identity monitoring service may be worth considering if you want more comprehensive monitoring and additional support when problems arise. Look for a plan that covers the types of activity most relevant to you and offers timely alerts. While no service can catch every form of identity theft, combining professional monitoring with your existing account security settings can give you an additional layer of protection. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at Cyberguy.com What to do if you find something unfamiliar Pro tip: Start with the four highest-impact places: If you only have a few minutes, check your email, bank accounts, phone account and credit reports first. Those areas can help reveal whether someone is trying to access your information, move money, receive verification codes or open new credit. A clean credit report does not rule out identity theft, so return to the other four places when you have time. YOUR BANK MAY STOP TEXTING YOU SIX-DIGIT CODES Kurt's key takeaways I think one of the biggest mistakes people make with identity theft is assuming that a clean credit report means they're in the clear. Someone could be using your information to open a phone line, get medical care or run up a utility bill, and you might not find out until much later. I'd start by checking your email, bank accounts and wireless carrier settings. Then pull your free credit reports and take a closer look at places you might normally overlook. I'm also a big believer in freezing your credit before there's a problem. It's free, and you can temporarily lift the freeze when you need to apply for credit. Identity monitoring can provide another layer of protection, but no service can monitor everything. That's why it's important to keep an eye on your accounts, too. The sooner you spot an unfamiliar account or transaction, the sooner you can start limiting the damage. articles.title: Neighbour fires 15 rounds, kills Singapore-based IT VP after parking spat in Faridabad
articles.summary: Faridabad parking dispute turns fatal: neighbor arrested after firing 15 rounds, killing Singapore-based IT VP Paramjeet Dhankar; dog feud also probed.
articles.body: Gurgaon: A neighbour allegedly pumped nine bullets into a senior IT executive during a parking dispute outside his Faridabad home on Friday night, killing him before he could be wheeled into a hospital. Paramjeet Dhankar (45), who was senior vice-president at Singapore-based FPT Software Company Ltd and former regional business head of Tech Mahindra’s Asia-Pacific operations, had returned home just a day earlier to attend his nephew’s wedding.The shooting took place around 8.30pm on Friday. According to a complaint lodged by Dhankar’s son, Shaurya, neighbour Mohan Sharma rang the bell at the family’s floor in Sector 21C and called Dhankar downstairs, asking him to move his car. Shaurya accompanied his father to the parking area, where an argument broke out. Mohan (44), a scrap dealer, allegedly whipped out his licensed pistol and opened fire at close range.Police said a total of 15 rounds were fired. Nine bullets are likely to have struck Dhankar, though the exact number will be confirmed only after autopsy. Mohan then allegedly fired at Shaurya, who escaped by taking cover behind parked vehicles. Dhankar tried to escape but collapsed and died at the spot. The accused fled in his car.Bloodstains marked the road where Dhankar fell, while bullet marks were visible on parking pillars and vehicles. Teams from Surajkund police station, the crime branch and forensic science laboratory secured the scene and collected evidence, including empty cartridges.The immediate confrontation, according to Shaurya’s complaint, was over car parking. Police are also examining whether a separate, long-running dispute over Mohan’s pet dog contributed to the hostility. Dhankar’s son had recently objected to the dog defecating in the common parking area. Police have not established whether this quarrel played a role in Friday’s shooting.The families lived in the same building and had a history of altercations. Mohan lived with his wife, son and daughter on the second floor of house No. 641, while Dhankar and his family occupied the ground floor. Police said they had frequently quarrelled over minor issues.Around five days before the murder, Mohan allegedly abused Shaurya during a disagreement over the pet dog. Dhankar’s family lodged a police complaint, but the matter was later settled.Dhankar’s father, Mange Ram, alleged that Mohan had also damaged the family’s house gate, prompting another complaint two-three days before the shooting. He further accused Mohan of recently assaulting an 85-year-old neighbour in the same building.“Mohan is a notorious man, and he recently assaulted another 85-year-old neighbour in the building. He had also damaged our house gate three days back, following which we lodged a police complaint as well. On Friday, he called my son downstairs on the pretext of asking him to move his car and fired at him, killing him on the spot. There is ample space in the parking area. My son was a very decent man,” Mange Ram said.A crime branch team arrested Mohan near DLF Chowk in Ballabhgarh on Saturday. “He was taken into custody following a search operation launched after the murder. He will be produced before a court and taken on remand for questioning and collection of evidence,” police spokesperson Yashpal Yadav said.Surajkund SHO Prahlad Kumar confirmed that 15 rounds were fired from Mohan’s gun. “After receiving information about the firing, police teams immediately reached the spot. The accused was arrested within a few hours,” he said.A case was registered at Surajkund police station under sections 103 (murder), 109 (attempt to murder) and 61(2) (criminal conspiracy) of BNS. The body was sent for autopsy.Dhankar had returned to Faridabad from Singapore on Nov 5 for his nephew’s wedding, scheduled for Nov 24. Originally from Hisar, he had moved to Faridabad with his family. His profile on LinkedIn lists him as a former head of Tech Mahindra’s Asia-Pacific regional business operations before joining FPT Software as senior vice-president.
